Max Planck was a German theoretical physicist widely regarded as the founder of quantum mechanics. He made a revolutionary proposal that fundamentally altered the course of modern physics: that energy is emitted or absorbed not continuously, but in discrete packets. This single insight opened the quantum age. He was awarded the 1918 Nobel Prize in Physics for his discovery of energy quanta.

Planck solved the ultraviolet catastrophe — a major crisis in late-nineteenth-century physics — by introducing the hypothesis that electromagnetic energy can only be emitted in quantized packets, not as a smooth wave. Classical physics predicted that hot objects should emit infinite energy at ultraviolet wavelengths, which obviously doesn't happen. Planck's quantum hypothesis solved this paradox.

He defined the Planck constant, approximately 6.626 times ten to the negative thirty-fourth Joule-seconds, a fundamental physical constant that relates the energy of a photon to its frequency through the equation E equals h times f. This constant is one of the most important numbers in physics.

Planck formulated Planck's law of black-body radiation, a mathematical formula that accurately describes the spectral density of electromagnetic radiation emitted by an object in thermal equilibrium — how much radiation is emitted at each frequency. He also established the Planck units, a system of natural measurement units based on fundamental physical constants: the Planck length, Planck time, and Planck mass. These units represent the smallest scales at which classical physics breaks down.

Planck served as president of the Kaiser Wilhelm Society during the interwar years and through World War II. After his death, the society was renamed the Max Planck Society in his honor, and it remains one of the world's leading research organizations. Albert Einstein built directly on Planck's quantum hypothesis when he explained the photoelectric effect. Niels Bohr incorporated the Planck constant into his groundbreaking quantized model of the hydrogen atom.
